questions.learningObjective: Explain how a chain of replies reorganises a set of documents.
questions.stem: A revised plan is compared with the draft it replaces, and the memo reads each as answering the one before.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that restoring four documents to a chain of replies means presenting each as a response to its predecessor, so that the comparison reveals a developing argument rather than four separate schemes. Read in sequence, the draft answers the consultation, the consultation answers the objection, the objection is answered by the revision, and the memo can say what each reply added and what it left standing.

questions.explanation: A chain of replies turns separate documents into an argument, because each is read against the one it answers. That reveals what changed and why, which a side-by-side comparison of versions cannot show.
questions.hint: Ask what each document is answering.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison held inside one form
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the strengths and limits of a comparison held inside one form.
questions.stem: One document type can hold a comparison only when every document being weighed is of that kind.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that holding a comparison inside one form is a deliberate restriction on what counts as evidence. It makes the comparison rigorous because every item has the same shape and can be tested on the same terms, but it also means that material of other kinds, which might have borne on the same question, is left out of the account. The memo should therefore say what the restriction has excluded as well as what it has included.

questions.explanation: A comparison inside one form is rigorous because the items share a shape, but it excludes other material silently unless the memo names the exclusion. Its strength and its cost are one fact.
questions.hint: Ask what the restriction leaves out.

questions.stem: A chronology of reforms is laid out in the appendix, and the officer says the order matters more than the entries.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that a chronological comparison assumes sequence is significant, so that the order of the entries already tells the reader how to judge them: the later reform responds to the earlier, and the earlier is treated as the condition the later addresses. questions.explanation: A chronological comparison smuggles in a judgement about sequence, so the dates do argumentative work beyond recording order. Because that judgement is rarely stated, it should be made explicit.

options.misconception: picks the principle by ease of production rather than purpose

options.text: The choice of principle follows from habit, since previous memos have always been arranged by theme.
options.misconception: defers the choice to departmental habit rather than the question

questions.explanation: The principle of organisation should follow the decision the committee must make, since theme and chronology answer different questions. Documents, convenience and habit do not settle which question is in play.
questions.hint: Ask which question the committee is actually deciding.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a chronological comparison assumes
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumption a chronological comparison makes.

stimulus.body: Reviewer: This table lists nine schemes by the year they were announced. Officer: That is the order the announcements came in. Reviewer: All right. But the reader will think the schemes respond to one another. Do you want them to?

questions.stem: A chronology is assumed in a table of schemes that never mentions why the order was chosen.

options.text: Chronological comparison assumes sequence carries significance, so the officer should publish the schemes in reverse order.
options.misconception: offers reversed order as the cure for the assumption

options.text: Chronological comparison assumes sequence carries significance, so the table proposes a story without saying so.
Chronological comparison assumes sequence carries significance, so the officer should add a paragraph on each scheme.
options.misconception: proposes more explanation rather than naming the assumption

options.text: Chronological comparison assumes sequence carries significance, so the reader is expected to object to the arrangement.
options.misconception: makes reader objection the expected response

questions.explanation: Arranging schemes by announcement date invites the reader to see each as responding to the last, whether intended or not. The remedy is to state what the order does, not to reverse it.
questions.hint: Ask what the order does without being explained.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Four novels restored to a chain of replies
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a chain of replies reorganises a set of documents.
questions.stem: Four documents in a folder appear to answer one another and the officer wants the committee to see it.

options.text: Presenting the four as replies makes the reader track a developing line rather than assess four options.
Presenting the four as replies makes the reader track a developing line, which saves the committee reading time.
options.misconception: justifies the arrangement by the time it saves readers

options.text: Presenting the four as replies makes the reader track a developing line, so the last option wins the argument.
options.misconception: treats the final reply as the winning option

options.text: Presenting the four as replies makes the reader track a developing line, so the committee should adopt them all.
options.misconception: slides from a presentation choice into a recommendation

questions.explanation: Arranging documents as replies gives the reader a line of development to follow rather than four items to judge separately. It is not a reason to adopt the last option or to save reading time.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader can now do that they could not before.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two principles compared, theme against chronology
questions.learningObjective: Compare a thematic principle of order with a chronological one.
questions.stem: Two of these documents share a series, and both happen to be annual reports.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that the choice between a thematic and a chronological arrangement has to do with the question the comparison is meant to answer, and that the identity of the documents does not settle it. Two annual reports can be compared by the aims they share, which shows how policy has been applied consistently, or by the order in which they appeared, which shows how one response became the next. The memo must choose because the two arrangements surface different relations.

questions.explanation: Sharing a series shows the documents are comparable in kind, but not which question to put to them. Arranging by aim or by sequence surfaces different relations, so the choice follows from the aim.
questions.hint: Ask which question the comparison is meant to answer.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison held inside one form
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the strengths and limits of a comparison held inside one form.
questions.stem: One comparison is kept within a single council memo and the committee objects that one side is missing.

options.text: A comparison restricted to one document omits what the other would show, so the restriction is a real limitation.
A comparison restricted to one document omits what the other would show, so the memo is plainly incomplete.
options.misconception: treats any restriction as proof the memo is incomplete

options.text: A comparison restricted to one document omits what the other would show, so the committee should ask for more documents.
options.misconception: answers the objection by calling for a larger evidence base

options.text: A comparison restricted to one document omits what the other would show, so the restriction is a limitation on evidence.
options.misconception: adds an unargued clause about evidence to a true statement

questions.explanation: Restricting a comparison to one document makes it coherent but leaves out what the excluded document would show, and that exclusion is a limitation, not a defect.
questions.hint: Ask what the excluded document would have shown.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A likeness drawn from two last pages
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the weight of a likeness drawn from two last pages.
questions.stem: Two reports are read in sequence and compared, and the reader notices their final paragraphs rhyme.

options.text: A likeness between the endings is evidence about how both reports close, worth noting but little else, and proves a shared author.
options.misconception: keeps the true statement and adds an unfounded conclusion

options.text: A likeness between the endings is evidence about how both reports close, worth noting but worth little alone.
A likeness between the endings is evidence about how both reports close, worth noting but little else, so ignore it.
options.misconception: draws a dismissal from the weakness of the evidence

options.text: A likeness between the endings is evidence about how both reports close, worth noting but little else, so compare the openings.
options.misconception: redirects the search to another part of the documents

questions.explanation: A resemblance at the end of two reports tells you about their presentation of conclusion and little more, since closings are conventional. It neither proves a shared author nor deserves dismissal.
questions.hint: Ask how conventional closings usually are.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a chronological comparison assumes
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumption a chronological comparison makes.
questions.stem: A planner argues that comparing by theme says more than comparing by date, and the committee asks why.

options.text: The claim is that theme exposes shared aims and conflicts that a date order hides, and it is simply correct.
options.misconception: adds an assertion of correctness to a claim about method

options.text: The claim is that theme exposes shared aims and conflicts that a date order hides, and dates are useless.
options.misconception: inflates a claim about emphasis into a dismissal of dates

options.text: The claim is that theme exposes shared aims and conflicts that a date order hides, so more is revealed.
The claim is that theme exposes shared aims and conflicts that a date order hides, so the memo should drop the chronology.
options.misconception: turns a claim about emphasis into a recommendation to omit

questions.explanation: The planner claims one arrangement surfaces more of a particular relation than another. That is a claim about emphasis; it neither makes chronology useless nor settles that theme is always better.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two readings of the same pair of texts
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two readers can read the same pair differently.

stimulus.body: Member: My reading is supported by the second paragraph of the report. Member: My reading is supported by the second paragraph of the report, and it says something quite different. Chair: Same paragraph? Member: Same paragraph.

questions.stem: Two groups of committee members read the same pair of documents and quote opposite sentences from them.

options.text: Two readings of one pair diverge because each reader supplies criteria the paragraph itself does not contain.
Two readings of one pair diverge because each supplies criteria the paragraph lacks, so one paragraph is badly written.
options.misconception: blames the paragraph for the divergence of readings

options.text: Two readings of one pair diverge because each supplies criteria the paragraph lacks, so the memo should choose one paragraph.
options.misconception: answers the divergence by choosing between two texts

options.text: Two readings of one pair diverge because each supplies criteria the paragraph lacks, so more paragraphs are needed.
options.misconception: answers the divergence by calling for more material

questions.explanation: When one sentence carries two opposed readings, the difference lies in what each reader takes the sentence to weigh. The paragraph need not be badly written, and more text would not resolve it.
questions.hint: Ask what each reader took the sentence to weigh.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison organised by a held-constant question
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a held-constant question organises a comparison.
questions.stem: A close reading compares the ending of one policy with the ending of another, and asks the same thing of both.

options.text: Applying the same question to both endings keeps the comparison steady, so any difference is a difference between them.
Applying the same question to both endings keeps the comparison steady, so any difference shows the question was poorly chosen.
options.misconception: treats any difference as proof the question was poor

options.text: Applying the same question to both endings keeps the comparison steady, so the endings must turn out to be similar.
options.misconception: treats a controlled comparison as guaranteeing similarity

options.text: Applying the same question to both endings keeps the comparison steady, so there can be no difference at all between them.
options.misconception: makes the controlled comparison produce no difference at all

questions.explanation: Asking the same thing of both endings keeps the test even, so any difference belongs to the endings rather than the method. It neither guarantees similarity nor indicts the question.
questions.hint: Ask what the shared question keeps even.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Four novels restored to a chain of replies
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a chain of replies reorganises a set of documents.
questions.stem: A final memo compares two strategies and notes that one appears to answer the other.

options.text: If one strategy answers the other, the pair is a chain of replies, so the later strategy is thereby correct.
options.misconception: treats a reply as proof that the later strategy is correct

options.text: If one strategy answers the other, the pair is a chain of replies, so the earlier strategy was thereby mistaken.
options.misconception: treats being answered as proof the earlier strategy failed

options.text: If one strategy answers the other, the pair is a chain of replies, so the two should be merged into one.
options.misconception: recommends merging the documents into a single plan

options.text: If one strategy answers the other, the pair is a chain of replies, and the comparison rests on that sequence.

questions.explanation: A strategy that answers another is read as a reply, turning the pair into a chain in which sequence matters. Answering proves neither correctness nor fault, and it does not require merging.
questions.hint: Ask what the reply relation makes of the sequence.
